extracted.intended_audience: practicing patent litigators, federal judges, and counsel handling equity actions in patent cases
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing interlocutory and final appeals, rehearings, bills of review, timing, required content/affidavits, and appellate scope in United States patent equity litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory appeal to Circuit Court of Appeals (30-day rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal from an interlocutory decree may in certain cases be taken to the Circuit Court of Appeals for the circuit in which that decree was rendered, at any time within thirty days from the entry of the decree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounds for such appeals have changed by statute over time; historically related to injunctions (granting, continuing, refusing, dissolving). See related statutory and case authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of interlocutory appeal (injunction-related review)
rubrics_metrics.description: On an interlocutory appeal relating to an injunction the Circuit Court of Appeals will decide the questions of validity and infringement, and whatever other questions underlie the question of the justice of an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If either validity or infringement decision is adverse to complainant, the appellate court may direct dismissal of the bill; factual findings of the court below have great weight and will stand unless obviously erroneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: No interlocutory appeal from accounting-only decree
rubrics_metrics.description: No appeal can be taken by a defendant from an interlocutory decree which directs an accounting of profits and damages, but does not order an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an interlocutory decree orders accounting and only orders an injunction as to part of the claims, the appellate court will not consider the part favorable to the defendant nor any part relating to the accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity Rule 69 — content and verification of rehearing petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every petition for rehearing shall contain the special matter or cause on which such rehearing is applied for, shall be signed by counsel, and the facts therein stated, if not apparent on the record, shall be verified by the oath of the party or by some other person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No rehearing shall be granted after the term at which the final decree was entered if an appeal lies; if no appeal lies the petition may be admitted before the end of the next term in the court's discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearing for matter apparent on record — required grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: A rehearing for matter apparent on the face of the record may be applied for by a petition signed by counsel and stating the ground upon which the rehearing is prayed; that ground must be sufficient to convince the judge that the decree was perhaps erroneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must point out a particular misapprehension of law or particular mistake in respect of the evidence. Cannot be established merely by omission to review all evidence or by general assertion that the decision is wrong. Court may sua sponte order rehearing if judge begins to doubt his decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearing for newly discovered evidence — timeliness and contents
rubrics_metrics.description: A rehearing on account of newly discovered evidence must be applied for as soon as possible after its discovery, by a petition verified by oath, stating the nature of the alleged newly discovered evidence, that it was not known until after the decree, and what diligence was exercised in searching for it prior to that time, and praying leave to file a supplemental bill in the nature of a bill of review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function is to furnish pleadings foundation for evidence on both sides; petition should seek leave to file supplemental bill and rehearing when issues are ready for hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit support for petitions based on new evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition for rehearing based on newly discovered evidence must be supported by affidavits of the witnesses who are expected to testify to the newly discovered facts, and also by affidavits showing that those facts were not discovered by the petitioner until after the former hearing and could not, with reasonable diligence, have been discovered sooner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opposing party may file counter-affidavits. To grant the petition, court must be satisfied that the applicant's affidavits are probably true, clearly material, and that the facts were not known and could not with reasonable diligence have been discovered — except the diligence point need not be shown where other party knew of the facts at decree time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearing will not be granted for fishing expeditions or counsel errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Rehearings will not be granted to enable parties to search for further evidence; nor to strengthen their expert testimony; nor to amend pleadings to make previously taken evidence admissible; nor to produce cumulative evidence on questions already in issue; nor to correct errors of management by petitioner's counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are firm limitations to prevent rehearings for mere tactical or evidentiary afterthoughts.

rubrics_metrics.name: No appeal from District Court decision on rehearing
rubrics_metrics.description: No appeal lies from a decision of a District Court granting or refusing any rehearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions for rehearing after appellate affirmation must be addressed to the appellate tribunal; denial by that tribunal is final, though it may grant permission to apply to the lower court for rehearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental bill in nature of bill of review — required allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: A supplemental bill in the nature of a bill of review should state the newly discovered facts upon which it is based and should pray that the cause may be heard with respect to the new matter at the same time that it is reheard upon the original bill, and that the party filing it may have such relief as the nature of his case requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceedings upon such a bill are the same as on original bills; rehearing after interlocutory decree does not stop an accounting unless court orders master to suspend; reversal may dismiss complainant's bill but allow use of master's evidence in later accounting; decree allocating costs before/after rehearing described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final decree for defendant — grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: A final decree will be entered in favor of the defendant where a demurrer to the whole bill is sustained or (since Equity Rules Feb 1, 1913) a motion to dismiss is granted on a point not cured by amendment; or where a plea to the whole bill or equivalent special matter in the answer is found true; or where certain defences applying to the whole bill are established at interlocutory hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple defenses exist, court may confine decision to any single sound defense; preference often given to non-infringement as basis rather than adjudicating patent validity, unless record establishes invalidity — in which case public interest favors declaring void patents void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference between non-infringement and invalidity rulings
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the defence of non-infringement is found, it is proper and generally preferable to base the decision for the defendant on that defense rather than adjudicating patent validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: complainant may lack motive to present full facts on validity. But where record contains enough to establish invalidity, it is proper and expedient to base decision on invalidity because the public has right to be judicially told a void patent is void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public character of litigation — no suppression of evidence on settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an action in equity for alleged infringement is settled after evidence is taken and before hearing, that settlement cannot include an effective stipulation that the evidence shall be withdrawn from the files of the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties must litigate in public and may not use tribunals to conceal or suppress records of their litigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single bill of costs when multiple cases use same evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Where several cases on one patent are litigated on one set of depositions and other evidence, only one bill of costs is taxed; where that bill is taxed against the complainant, a decree is made in favor of each defendant for an equal share of the amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical allocation rule when common evidence supports multiple defendant cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bill of review — two kinds (apparent errors vs newly discovered facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill of review is the proper means of securing reconsideration of a final decree after the term at which it was entered. Such bills are of two sorts: those filed to correct errors apparent on the face of the pleadings or decree; and those filed to introduce evidence of facts which occurred or were discovered after the decree was entered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each sort has different procedural prerequisites and time limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bill of review for apparent errors — filing time and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill of review to correct errors apparent on the pleadings or decree may be filed without leave of court, but will not be considered unless filed within the same time after entry of the decree as is provided for appeals (presently six months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a bill is confined to examination of the pleadings and decree; no bill lies to correct errors of fact made in weighing evidence on which the decree was based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bill of review for new facts — leave required and appellate procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill of review filed to introduce evidence of new facts cannot be filed without leave of court. Where the case has been appealed and decided by the Circuit Court of Appeals, the application for leave must be presented to that tribunal, which may authorize the lower court to receive and adjudicate the bill of review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mode of application: petition stating original proceedings and new facts, supported by affidavits showing materiality and sufficiency and that facts occurred after the decree or could not have been discovered earlier with reasonable diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for petitions to file bill of review based on discovered facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitions for leave to file a bill of review based on newly discovered facts may be filed more than six months after entry of decree provided they are filed within a reasonable time after the discovery upon which they are based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court will judge timeliness in light of when discovery occurred and reasonable diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: When leave to file bill of review will be denied
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave to file such a bill will not be granted where the facts stated are not adapted or sufficient to have altered the decree if before the court, nor where those facts could with reasonable diligence have been discovered before the decree, nor to enable impeachment of witness character or to introduce cumulative testimony on points already litigated and decided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newly discovered corroborating written evidence may, however, furnish a foundation for leave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure after filing bill of review for new facts
rubrics_metrics.description: After such a bill has been duly filed the opposite party may answer and thus put the filer to proof of its allegations; a motion to dismiss is not appropriate because legal sufficiency must be passed before filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The filer must be prepared to prove materiality and the facts supporting leave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bill in the nature of a bill of review — who may file
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill in the nature of a bill of review differs only in the legal character of the complainant: a bill of review can be filed by either party to the decree or their privies, while the bill in the nature of a bill of review is required where privies in estate (devisees or assignees) seek reversal after term expiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse with supplemental bills in the nature of bills of review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to Supreme Court in patent jurisdiction questions
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal to the Supreme Court can be taken by a complainant whose action for patent infringement has been dismissed by a District Court on the ground of want of jurisdiction; other appellate routes (certification from Circuit Court of Appeals) may be used to present jurisdiction questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice historically involved appeals to Circuit Court of Appeals and certification of jurisdictional questions to the Supreme Court; later authorities allow Circuit Courts to decide jurisdiction where assignments of error address it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limits for appeals to Circuit Court of Appeals (six months) and supersedeas rules
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal to a Circuit Court of Appeals is demandable from the final decree of any United States District Court in patent cases if taken within six months after entry of the decree; to operate as a supersedeas (stay execution) an appeal must be taken within sixty days after rendition of the decree; execution may be issued if appeal is not taken within ten days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A supersedeas obtained later prevents further proceedings under execution but does not undo what was already done. Time to appeal may be considered to begin when case is finally decided or when formal decree is signed and filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of supersedeas (what it stays and what it does not)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an appeal operates as a supersedeas it operates only as against the money recovery provided for in the decree and not as against the part directing payment of the master's fees, nor as against that part directing an injunction to issue; however the judge who enters a decree granting an injunction has discretion to suspend, modify or restore it pending appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effect: money recoveries are stayed; other parts may not be automatically stayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate appealability of certain district court decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: A decision of a District Court not to dismiss a bill for infringement upon motion of a nominal complainant (over opposition of those equitably entitled) is immediately appealable to the Circuit Court of Appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But a decree sustaining some claims and dismissing others is not appealable by the complainant as final until accounting has occurred and a completely final decree disposes of the entire case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-appealability of certain interlocutory decrees (expired patent/accounting)
rubrics_metrics.description: An interlocutory decree awarding merely an accounting and granting no injunction because the patent has expired is not appealable to the Circuit Court of Appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat such decrees as not appealing under injunction-related statutes when the patent's expiration makes injunction issues moot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation of the appellate record — transcript and stipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The prosecution of an appeal includes procuring from the clerk of the District Court a transcript of the record of the case, or of such parts as the parties agree are sufficient. Such an agreement must be a formal stipulation filed with the clerk; the clerk then prepares and certifies the transcript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stipulation to limit transcript scope where appropriate; ensure formal filing so clerk can act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals from District of Columbia courts in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal to the Court of Appeals of the District of Columbia is demandable from the final decree of the Supreme Court of the District of Columbia in any case arising under the patent laws; many rules applicable to U.S. District Court appeals also apply, with differences arising from statutory distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check specific statutory differences for DC courts' appellate jurisdiction; consult cited statutes and authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of review in Circuit Court of Appeals — permissible grounds and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: On hearing of an appeal in any Circuit Court of Appeals the decree may be attacked by the appellant upon any ground upon which it was resisted in the court below; the appellee may support it upon any ground in the record whether the lower court based its decree upon that ground or another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However the decree cannot be assailed on matters committed to judicial discretion (e.g., allowance/refusal of rehearing), or for certain procedural acts of the lower court such as refusal to set aside default decrees or errors made by a master in matters within his province.
